newsitem.title: USA: Ethics chair wants to meet soon about Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Ethics chair wants to meet soon about Gingrich.

text.p: The House Ethics Committee chairwoman wants the group to meet soon to recommend a penalty for Speaker Newt Gingrich, who has admitted giving inaccurate information, an aide said on Monday.
One committee member said the challenge was to find the first date that all members can attend.

Under House rules, the ethics committee recommends a penalty for a vote of the full House. House Republicans, who have a 20-vote majority, have said they would like to see the penalty phase concluded before Gingrich goes up for re-election to his House leadership post on Jan. 7.
Representative Nancy Johnson, a Connecticut Republican who chairs the ethics committee, would like to conduct the "sanctions hearing" soon, spokesman Ted Van Der Meid said.
"It's the goal of the chairwoman to wrap it up as quickly as possible, (but) the committee has no plans to meet this week," he said.

Both Republicans and Democrats said that any penalty was unlikely to topple Gingrich from his position, which is second in line to the presidency. Gingrich would be the first Republican speaker to be re-elected in 68 years.

Gingrich on Saturday admitted he provided inaccurate information to the ethics committee and accepted responsibility for failing to seek advice on whether a college course he taught complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt foundations for partisan purposes.

Options open to the committee range from doing nothing to expelling Gingrich from the House. A censure would essentially mean Gingrich would have to step down as speaker but could remain a member of the House.
"There's a fairly large menu of sanctions possible," Porter Goss, a Republican from Florida and a member of the ethics committee, said in a telephone interview.
"Frankly it's a logistics question of finding 10 members and their travel schedules and trying to find the first available date when they can all be in Washington," Goss said.
The committee has five Republicans and five Democrats. Six members must be present for a quorum. Congressional Republicans generally back Gingrich.

But Ohio Republican Representative Steve Chabot said he was not certain he would back the speaker's re-election. "I'm certainly concerned about the admissions and the facts that have come out, but I'm going to reserve my judgment (before making a decision)," Chabot said.
